s1.li1: Influential States or economic powers: they maintain diplomatic relations in the form of bilateral investment Agreements with African States;
s1.li2: International financial institutions: the World Bank, the IMF, the African Development Bank (AfDB), as well as the African Union, are key players in the financing of FDI projects in Africa, driven by a commitment to the economic progress of the continent;
s1.li3: Large commercial companies or multinationals: they seek to expand their activities in Africa or to export their goods to the African market.
s1.li5: Respect for and protection of intellectual property rights;
s1.li6: Risk reduction and legal security in the event of political conflicts;
s1.li7: Administrative flexibility, reflected in the absence of bureaucratic burdens.
s1.p1: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Africa refers to financial flows originating from foreign players or entities, intended to be invested in Africa. These flows aim to support profit-generating projects, to establish new economic activities or to improve the efficiency of existing activities. As a result, FDI fosters international economic cooperation, while bringing mutual benefits to investors and African countries.
s1.p2: The purpose of FDI in Africa is to stimulate the economic growth of the continent and to foster development in key areas such as health, education, agriculture, industry, infrastructure, technology, energy and welfare actions fighting hunger, among others.
s1.p3: In short, these investments improve living conditions, strengthen the competitiveness of African economies and foster solid and sustainable economic integration. In addition, they drive the growth of local skills and the sharing of knowledge.
s1.p4: FDI in Africa is financed by several players, namely:
s1.p5: The implementation of FDI initiatives or Projects, carried by investor players, may be undertaken through primary recourse to the national development agencies of African States, in order to benefit from support in the execution and management of the initiatives carried.
s1.p6: However, failing this approach, investor players can also collaborate with the specialised private sector, in particular the firm International HRM (International Human Resources Management), to benefit from the following reassuring advantages:
s1.p7: The firm International HRM is mandated to plan and organise the realisation of the projects carried by the FDI investor players in Africa, which places it in the position of needing associated partners in the countries of Africa, for the establishment of the various projects. International HRM, through its expertise, subcontracts its services to governments, international players and international projects.

s1.title: Overview of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Africa
s2.h1: FDI is a solution for Sustainable Development in Africa
s2.h2: Economic Growth of FDI in Africa
s2.h3: FDI impacts the poor populations of Africa
s2.p1: Africa is considered an emerging market with great consumption potential. In response to this momentum, African governments offer tax advantages and create favourable environments to attract foreign investors. These initiatives aim to foster sustainable development, while addressing the economic and social challenges of the continent.
s2.p2: In recent years, FDI destined for Africa has experienced a significant increase, with particular attention paid to the infrastructure and energy sectors. These investments not only boost economic production, but also improve the competitiveness of the continent on world markets.
s2.p3: The investor players of FDI initiatives in Africa are also required to play a social role through Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR). They actively contribute to projects that improve access to water, health care and quality education, thereby strengthening the foundations of sustainable development in Africa. These are essential actions, both for the populations of Africa and for international stability.
s2.title: Some facts about Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Africa
s3.p1: The projects financed by the FDI players in Africa, and mandated to International HRM, address essential sectors such as the fight against hunger, health, education, agriculture, industry, infrastructure, technology and energy, among others. Thus, partnership relations are engaged for each African country.
s3.p2: African executives, residing in their Countries or in the Diaspora, are invited, without distinction of professional qualifications, for beneficial partnerships, with the aim of fostering the proper execution of the FDI initiatives or Projects, which will be initiated in their Nations.
s3.title: Census of associated partners by International HRM

s4.title: Missions
s5.li1: Freedom and flexibility in time management, for the missions.
s5.li2: Remuneration calculated as a percentage of the profit, drawn from the Projects' execution budget.
s5.li3: Maturing experience and broadening professional relationships.
s5.li4: Private social security coverage (Family Health Insurance, Professional risk Insurance, End-of-partnership Indemnities).
s5.li5: Professional vehicle + Mission and housing allowances.
s5.title: Partners' privileges
s6.li2: Prerequisites: without distinction of professional qualifications. (Initial training in preparation for the partnership will be provided).
s6.li4: Contract duration: 7-year partnership contract (to complete the projects).
s6.li5: Nature: paid part-time offer, which does not require interrupting personal occupations. (Parallel source of profitability).
s6.li6: Mission location: the partner operates in the projects oriented towards his Country. However, he may work internationally if he so wishes.
s6.li7: Others: retired executives or those of the Diaspora are also involved.
